note: Player-facing help text shared by all four builds. patch-v9.py embeds it in the bundle. The house style applies, and test/guide.test.js checks it.

how.title: Tiers
how.intro: Tier sets the difficulty. The record sets a tier for each operation, and free play lets you pick another.

items.label: Tiers 1 to 6
items.text: Higher tiers are harder on the whole. Each step up shortens the clock to Consume, enlarges the opponent's base hand or starts the opponent with more pressure. From Tier 2 the opponent starts with pressure on the lever. From Tier 3 it starts on every domain in play.

items.label: Tier 7
items.text: Tier 7 sits above Tier 6. The clock to Consume runs one point shorter than at Tier 6. A fourth card joins the opponent's hand from turn 3, and every domain in play opens at 2 pressure. On most operations a scripted player rarely wins it.

items.label: Where tiers apply
items.text: Free play offers every tier. The campaign climbs from Tier 1 to Tier 6 along each arc. The daily runs at Tier 3. A win scores 100 more for each tier you climb.

items.label: Difficulty labels
items.text: Each tier of each operation carries a label from Gentle to Brutal. The label reads the share of 400 games a simple scripted player won at that tier. People may do better or worse.

how.title: Holdings
how.intro: Some operations give your side ground it must pay to keep. The Holdings panel lists each one.

items.label: Cost and denial
items.text: A holding charges you its cost every turn. The cost comes off your shields in its domain first and then lands as pressure. While you keep a holding it denies the rival part of its leverage.

items.label: Consuming
items.text: A holding turns consuming when its cost is more than what it denies. Every turn you keep a consuming holding counts as an act against your own position.

items.label: Giving one up
items.text: Give up a holding for 1 action. It stops costing you and stops denying the rival. Some holdings cost legitimacy to give up. You cannot take a holding back.

how.title: Reach and permits
how.intro: Some operations list acts with a strong effect. Each act carries a permit for your side, and the Reach panel shows it.

items.label: Open
items.text: An open act works at no price. Use it for the actions it names, up to its limit.

items.label: Has a price
items.text: A priced act works but costs your side legitimacy. The game counts it as an act against your own position, and it often helps the rival.

items.label: Closed to you
items.text: A closed act stays open to the rival and barred to your side. The panel still lists it. Open Why to read the evidence cards behind the permit.

items.label: The report
items.text: When the run ends the report counts each closed act the rival used. Permits are the game's reading of the evidence and not a count of anything.

how.title: Forecast
how.intro: The Forecast page lists claims from the book's prediction ledger. The ledger dated each claim before anyone knew how it would resolve.

items.label: Your forecast
items.text: Enter your chance that a claim holds, from 1 to 99 percent. Lock it before the check date. A locked forecast cannot change.

items.label: The score
items.text: When the result is in the game scores you with the Brier score. The score is the square of the miss, so lower is better. You see the book's own probability and a cheap reference answer beside yours.

items.label: Where results come from
items.text: The site owner copies each result from the project's scoring log. The page only mirrors that log. A few claims prove little.

factions.text: This panel shows every side in the operation. Each rival banks its own leverage toward Consume. Legitimacy falls with some acts and recovers on a coherent turn. Below the marked line a faction suffers an entropy spike.

leaders.text: A leader stands in one domain and changes the rules there. Read the line under each name. Move each of yours once a turn for 1 action.

holdings.text: Each holding costs you every turn and keeps some leverage from the rival. A holding marked consuming costs more than it denies. Give it up when it stops paying.

reach.text: Each act here carries a permit for your side. Open acts cost nothing extra. Priced acts work and cost legitimacy. Closed acts stay barred to you, and Why shows the evidence.

tier7.text: You are playing Tier 7, the top tier. Every domain in play opens at 2 pressure and the opponent's hand grows sooner. On most operations a scripted player rarely wins here.

difficulty.won: A scripted player won {n} percent of its games at this tier.
difficulty.note: Each label reads the share of games a simple scripted player won. People may do better or worse.

ui.glossIntro: The terms the board and its panels use. A term shows here when this build has the rule behind it.

glossary.text: Each move costs actions, shown as blue dots on the board. Most operations give 3 a turn and 1 more for every 2 points of coherence. Two or more left unspent at the end of a turn can cost coherence.
One of the twelve fields the contest runs through, from Kinetic to Data and Surveillance. Each domain holds pressure and shields. Bold outlines mark the domains in play.
Strain on a domain, from 0 to 5. At 3 or more the domain pays the opponent 1 leverage each turn. At 5 the domain falls and pays 2.
A shield absorbs 1 pressure. Defend adds one for 1 action.
Pressure that grows by itself each turn until you clear it. Disrupt on the domain clears slopes before pressure.
What the opponent banks from domains under strain. Leverage moves the operation along its lifecycle toward Consume.
The five stages of an operation. Attract leads to Accommodate, then Control and Extract, and last to Consume.
The last stage. The opponent wins when the operation reaches Consume before the clock runs out.
The one domain an operation turns on. You may name it once. A right guess cuts leverage by 2 and makes Disrupts there cost 1 less. A wrong guess gives the opponent 2 and costs coherence.

How well your side acts as one, from 0 to 5. A turn with a shield that absorbs a hit, a Disrupt on a card you detected or a right lever raises it by 1. A turn with two idle actions or a fallen domain lowers it by 1. A turn with both changes nothing.
Costs 1 action and reveals a hidden card.
Costs 2 actions, and 1 less at a named lever. On a card you can name it cancels the card and captures it for your codex. On a domain it clears slopes and then pressure.
Costs 1 action and adds a shield to a domain.
A move the opponent aims at a domain. The card lands when you end the turn unless you disrupt it.
A card that shows nothing. Detect it before you answer it.
A card that shows a threat and hides its name. The threat may be a feint.
A false card that holds nothing. Detect shows it for what it is.
A card that pays you now and costs you now or later. Leave it and it passes.
A domain where you hold no authority yet, marked GATED. Spend 1 action to open the gate before you act there.
A domain the operation leans on, marked LOAD. Under Criticality the opponent aims there more often. A fall there moves the operation a full stage.
The physics an operation runs under, one of ten. Each dimension changes one rule and names a counter.
An optional bonus tied to one dimension. Attribution, the Asymmetry lens, is open from the start. Win an operation under a dimension to unlock its lens. Boot camp and guided runs unlock none.
A card you may play once per operation. Each one unlocks at a level.
The difficulty of a run, from 1 to 7. The record sets a tier for each operation, and free play lets you pick another.
The top tier, above Tier 6. Every domain in play opens at 2 pressure.
A label from Gentle to Brutal on each operation and tier. The label reads the share of 400 games a simple scripted player won there. People may do better or worse.
One star means you held the line. Two mean the operation stopped before Extract. Three mean you cut the lever or kept leverage under 40 percent.
A side in an operation. Each faction has its own pressure and shields in every domain.
A faction's standing, from 0 to 100. Some acts cost it and a coherent turn restores it. Below 25 a faction suffers an entropy spike.
What a faction suffers below 25 legitimacy. Its own domains start to come apart.
A figure or an office that stands in one domain and changes the rules there. Move each of yours once a turn for 1 action.
An agreement between factions. Members do not target each other while it holds. Some pacts stand against a third faction.
Cards aimed at the other factions. You cannot answer them, but they shift the balance between the others.
Ground your side pays to keep. A holding costs you every turn and denies the rival part of its leverage.
A holding whose cost is more than what it denies. Each turn you keep it counts as an act against your own position.
A move that weakens the side that makes it. The report lists each one with its type.
An act with a strong effect that carries a permit for your side.
Open, priced or closed. Open acts cost nothing extra. Priced acts cost legitimacy. Closed acts stay barred to you. Each permit is the game's reading of its evidence cards.
A card that states one claim in the game's own words, with an id such as EV-001. The project keeps the source for each card, and some still wait for a check.

The three 2026 operations whose acts carry permits. The rival acts with no court, no press and no vote in the way. Some acts are closed to your side and some carry a price. They play at Tier 7 on the record.
An operation on a subject that has not settled yet. It plays the record up to its last source.
Your chance, from 1 to 99 percent, that a dated claim holds. Lock it before the check date.
The square of the miss between your chance and the result. Lower is better.
A plain guess from a stated basis, such as a base rate. The game scores it beside you and the book.
A line that holds the seed and every action of a run. The game replays it to check the score.
A finished run played back step by step from its result code.
A link that fixes the operation, the tier and the seed, so two players face the same opening.
One operation for every player each day, at Tier 3. Your first finished run of the day counts.
A chain of operations that climbs from Tier 1 to Tier 6. Win one to open the next.
Your collection of the 36 stratagems. Disrupt a card to capture it.
Six turns at The Gate at Canton in 1784 that teach the board.
A short run of one operation at Tier 1 with coach steps. Each one teaches one panel.
A domain marked LOCK, where you cannot disrupt until the count runs out. One stratagem card sets the lock.
A card marked PROXY, delivered through a third party. Disrupting it costs 1 more action. Where legitimacy is in play the faction that plays it loses some.
A setting some operations run in, shown after the tier. Long Grind adds a turn and moves Consume 2 points later, and Unwinding moves it 2 sooner. Runaway and Machine Mandate feed the opponent's hand.
